related_questions.question: How accurate are home COVID tests?

text_blocks.snippet: Home COVID-19 tests are generally reliable for detecting positive cases, especially when symptoms are present, but may be less accurate for detecting asymptomatic infections. Repeat testing is recommended following a negative result to reduce the chance of a false negative.

list.title: Positive results are reliable:
list.snippet: If an at-home test indicates a positive result, it's highly likely that the individual has COVID-19, according to the CDC and the FDA.

list.title: Negative results require caution:
list.snippet: At-home antigen tests are less sensitive than PCR tests and may not always detect the virus, especially in the early stages of infection or in people without symptoms.

list.title: Importance of repeat testing:
list.snippet: The FDA and CDC recommend repeating a negative test 48 hours after the initial negative result to increase the chances of detecting the virus if it is present, says Harvard Health.

list.title: Symptomatic vs. asymptomatic:
list.snippet: A study published in Microbiology Spectrum found that at-home tests are more effective at detecting COVID-19 when individuals have symptoms.

list.title: False negatives:
list.snippet: If a person has symptoms but tests negative on an at-home test, they should continue to isolate and consider repeating the test or getting a PCR test.

text_blocks.snippet: To perform an at-home COVID-19 rapid antigen test, carefully read the instructions provided with your specific test kit, as not all tests are the same. Generally, you will collect a nasal sample using a swab, mix it with a solution, and then apply the mixture to a test strip or device. A positive result usually indicates a likely COVID-19 infection. If you get a negative result but have symptoms, you may still need to consider other testing options.

list.title: 1. Gather your supplies:
list.snippet: This includes the test kit, a timer, and any additional materials listed in the instructions.

list.title: 2. Prepare the test:
list.snippet: This may involve opening the test device, mixing a solution, or preparing the swab.

list.title: 3. Collect the sample:
list.snippet: Follow the instructions carefully to collect the nasal sample. This usually involves inserting the swab into one nostril and rotating it several times.

list.title: 4. Process the sample:
list.snippet: Apply the sample to the test device as instructed.

list.title: 5. Read the results:
list.snippet: After the specified time, read the results on the test device. A positive result will typically show two lines, while a negative result will show one.

list.title: 6. Follow up:
list.snippet: If you test positive, isolate yourself and follow the guidance of your local health authority. If you test negative but have symptoms, consider retesting or consulting a healthcare professional.
